newsitem.title: USA: Strong dollar hurts Dow Chemical results.
newsitem.headline: Strong dollar hurts Dow Chemical results.

text.p: Dow Chemical Co. said Thursday the strong dollar contributed to a 5 percent decline in its first quarter earnings, but the results still exceeded Wall Street estimates.
Dow earned $452 million, or $1.90 a share, compared with year-earlier earnings of $476 million, which also was equal to $1.90 a share due to stock repurchases in the past year.

Dow said the dollar's strength reduced its sales and operating earnings by about $100 million during the quarter. Revenues were flat at $4.99 billion despite 2 percent growth in product volume during the January to March period.

"The strong U.S. dollar played a significant role in the price decline we experienced in the first quarter," Dow Chief Executive Officer William Stavropoulos said in a statement. "However, when we adjust for this currency impact, we actually see positive pricing trends in many of our key products from both a year ago and the previous quarter."

Analysts had predicted that the chemical giant would earn about $1.72 a share, according to First Call Corp. The $1.90 a share earnings sent Dow's stock up $2.125 to close at $81.875 Thursday on the New York Stock Exchange.

PaineWebber analyst Andrew Cash attributed the earnings surprise in part to mild spring weather in the United States, which increased demand for polyvinyl chloride plastics used in the construction industry.
"One of the most positive things was their 'capital temperance,'" Cash added. "They're not out there spending money willy nilly."
Dow's capital expenditures during the quarter dropped to $245 million from $264 million in the year-ago period.
Cash noted, however, that continued global overcapacity in ethylene-based products -- which account for up to one-third of Dow's sales -- will continue to pressure the company's stock.

Dow's earnings were also hurt by a $230 million increase in hydrocarbon raw material costs that offset $200 million in operating profit improvements due to cost cutting, productivity gains, restructuring and acqusitions.
The Midland, Mich.-based company said it expects a more favourable climate for raw material costs and product prices in the second quarter, but not as good as a year ago.
"As we head into the second quarter, favourable global economic conditions will support solid volume growth in our businesses," Stavropoulos said.

"Lower feedstock costs and price stability in some key products, coupled with the on-going implementation of our productivity and value-growth initiatives, should result in a strong quarter for Dow," he said.
